lessonTitle: Types of Automation: Fixed, Programmable and Flexible

blocks.text: A car-engine plant machines the same cylinder block every 40 seconds, 24 hours a day, on a 60 m long line of stations linked by a transfer bar. Next door a job shop machines 300 different aerospace brackets in batches of five. Both are automated, yet they could not swap equipment. The choice of automation level is an economic and engineering match between how many parts you make and how many different parts you make.

blocks.markdown: Automation means equipment that performs operations with little or no direct human effort. Three levels are distinguished by how easily the machine changes from one part to another. This split is the standard one used in production-systems texts, and the boundaries are fuzzy in real plants, so the test is always: *what must be done to change the part, and how long does it take?*

blocks.title: Fixed, programmable and flexible automation
blocks.text: **Fixed (hard) automation**: the sequence of operations is fixed by the equipment configuration (cams, transfer lines, dedicated tooling). **Programmable automation**: the sequence is controlled by a program that can be changed, but the machine must be stopped for a changeover (loading the new program, tools and fixtures) between batches. **Flexible automation**: an extension of programmable automation in which changeover is so quick (often fully automatic, with programs, tools and fixtures called up by the controller) that different parts can be mixed in sequence with essentially no lost production time.

blocks.markdown: **Why volume and variety decide.** Fixed automation has a large up-front cost that is spread over many parts, so it wins only when the annual quantity is large and the design is stable. Programmable automation has a lower fixed cost but a higher cost per part, so it wins at lower quantities. Where variety is high and quantity per variety is low, manual or stand-alone programmable methods are used, because dedicated equipment for each variety could never be paid back.

blocks.caption: Annual cost per part: F is the annual fixed cost (equipment cost divided by life, in currency units per year), Q is the annual quantity (parts per year), v is the variable cost per part (currency units per part).

blocks.title: Break-even quantity between fixed and programmable automation
blocks.prompt: A dedicated transfer line costs 600 000 currency units (cu), lasting 5 years with no residual value, and has variable cost $v=0.40$ cu per part. A programmable CNC cell costs 250 000 cu over the same life with $v=1.30$ cu per part. Find the annual quantity at which the two cost the same. Ignore interest.

steps.text: Annual fixed cost of each option is equipment cost divided by life.
Equate the annual total cost $F+vQ$ for the two options.
Solve the linear equation for the annual quantity $Q$.

blocks.answer: About 77 800 parts per year; above this the dedicated line is cheaper, below it the programmable cell is cheaper.

blocks.markdown: **Robot versus dedicated tooling for loading.** A pick-and-place machine or chute feeder designed for one part (dedicated tooling) is fast, simple and cheap for a single product, but must be rebuilt or replaced when the part changes. An industrial robot with a gripper is slower for a single repetitive move but is reprogrammable and can be fitted with different grippers, so it serves several part families with the same capital outlay. The robot also tolerates part-position variation better when fitted with sensors.

blocks.title: How many part families justify a robot loader?
blocks.prompt: A robot loader costs 90 000 cu with a 5 year life (annual cost 18 000 cu). A dedicated loader for one part family costs 35 000 cu with a 5 year life (7 000 cu per year per family); each additional family needs its own loader. Operating costs and cycle time are assumed equal. For how many families do the annual costs match?

steps.text: Annual cost of the robot is independent of the number of families $n$.
Annual cost of dedicated loaders grows with $n$.
Equate the two annual costs and solve for the number of families.

blocks.answer: Break-even at about 2.6 families: with three or more part families the robot is cheaper; with one or two the dedicated loaders are cheaper.

items: Volume high, variety one: fixed automation (transfer line).
Volume medium, variety medium, batches with changeover: programmable automation (CNC machine, robot cell).
Variety high with mixed models and short runs: flexible automation, or manual and stand-alone machines if volume is very small.
The robot wins on reprogrammability; dedicated tooling wins on speed and cost when the product never changes.

blocks.title: The deciding question
blocks.text: Ask first how often the part changes and what a changeover costs in lost production time. Fixed automation has an enormous changeover cost, programmable has a moderate one, and flexible has almost none.

blocks.title: A common misreading
blocks.text: Automation does not equal flexibility. A fully automatic, unmanned transfer line is still fixed automation if changing the product requires rebuilding the line.

points: Classify automation by changeover: fixed (retooling needed), programmable (reprogram and reset between batches), flexible (negligible changeover, mixed parts).
Select the level from volume and variety: high volume and one part to fixed, medium batches to programmable, high variety to flexible, very low volume to manual or stand-alone CNC.
A robot loader trades speed for reprogrammability; its cost advantage over dedicated tooling grows with the number of part families.

questions.stem: A line machines one model of crankshaft at 90 per hour, 24 hours a day. Workpieces move automatically between 14 stations by a transfer bar, and each station has special-purpose cutting heads that cannot be repurposed without rebuilding. How is this line classified?

options.text: Fixed automation, because the operation sequence is built into dedicated equipment
Programmable automation, because the line is automatic
Flexible automation, because it runs unmanned around the clock
Manual production, because the product never changes

questions.correctOptionText: Fixed automation, because the operation sequence is built into dedicated equipment

distractorRationale.a: The sequence is fixed by special-purpose heads and a transfer bar, which is the signature of fixed automation.
distractorRationale.b: Being automatic does not make a line programmable; programmable automation means the sequence can be changed by a program.
distractorRationale.c: Unmanned running is unrelated to flexibility; flexible automation requires negligible changeover between different parts.
distractorRationale.d: One product does not imply manual work; the line is fully mechanised.

questions.explanation: Dedicated stations that cannot be repurposed without rebuilding are the signature of fixed automation. The product never changes and the volume is very high, which is exactly where a high up-front investment pays back.

questions.stem: A machining centre runs a stored program to make a batch of 200 flanges. Between batches an operator loads a new program, swaps the tools and changes the fixture, which takes about 3 hours. How is this operation classified?

options.text: Fixed automation, because one machine makes one batch at a time
Flexible automation, because it uses numerical control
Programmable automation, because the sequence is changed by a program but changeover stops production
Manual production, because an operator changes the fixture

questions.correctOptionText: Programmable automation, because the sequence is changed by a program but changeover stops production

distractorRationale.a: Fixed automation needs physical rebuilding; here a new program and tool set suffices.
distractorRationale.b: Flexible automation needs negligible changeover; 3 hours lost per batch is not negligible.
distractorRationale.c: A changeable program with a stop for tools and fixture is programmable automation.
distractorRationale.d: The operator only sets up; the cutting cycle itself is automatic under program control.

questions.explanation: The three-hour changeover separates programmable from flexible automation: production stops while the new program, tools and fixture are installed. Since this changeover is by program and not by rebuilding, it is not fixed automation either.

questions.stem: A company must produce 40 different hydraulic fittings, each in a yearly quantity of only a few hundred, and the designs change every year. Which automation level is the most appropriate economically?

options.text: Programmable or flexible automation (CNC machines), because variety is high and each volume is small
A dedicated transfer line for each fitting, because automation always cuts cost per part
One high-volume transfer line shared by all 40 fittings
No machines at all, because low volumes cannot justify any equipment

questions.correctOptionText: Programmable or flexible automation (CNC machines), because variety is high and each volume is small

distractorRationale.a: High variety and low volume per variety favour reprogrammable machines.
distractorRationale.b: A dedicated line per fitting could never recover its cost from a few hundred parts a year.
distractorRationale.c: A transfer line is fixed to one part; it cannot be shared across 40 designs.
distractorRationale.d: Programmable CNC machines have moderate cost per part and are the standard way to serve low-volume high-variety work.

questions.explanation: The cost of dedicated tooling would be spread over only a few hundred parts and would be obsolete after a design change. Programmable (or flexible) CNC machines amortise a single investment across all 40 fittings.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes flexible automation from programmable automation?

options.text: Flexible automation uses no computer control, while programmable automation does
Flexible automation changes between different parts with negligible lost time, so different parts can be mixed in sequence
Flexible automation is cheaper per part than fixed automation at any volume
Flexible automation can make only one product, but faster

questions.correctOptionText: Flexible automation changes between different parts with negligible lost time, so different parts can be mixed in sequence

distractorRationale.a: Both rely on computer control; flexible automation uses more of it, not less.
distractorRationale.b: Negligible changeover and mixed-part sequencing define flexible automation.
distractorRationale.c: Fixed automation has the lowest unit cost at very high volume; flexible automation does not beat it there.
distractorRationale.d: One product at high speed describes fixed automation.

questions.explanation: Both levels are programmable, but in programmable automation the machine stops for changeover between batches. Flexible automation removes that loss, so a model mix can run continuously.

questions.stem: A cell must load castings from a pallet into a lathe. Three part families, each with a different shape and size, will be run on the same lathe over the year. Which loading method is justified and why?

options.text: An industrial robot, because it is reprogrammable and can change grippers for different families
Three dedicated loaders, because dedicated tooling is always cheaper
A single dedicated loader, because the parts are all castings
Manual loading, because robots cannot load heavy castings

questions.correctOptionText: An industrial robot, because it is reprogrammable and can change grippers for different families

distractorRationale.a: Three families with different shapes favour a reprogrammable robot with changeable grippers.
distractorRationale.b: Dedicated tooling is cheaper only for few families; each extra family needs its own equipment.
distractorRationale.c: The shapes and sizes differ, so one dedicated loader cannot handle all three families.
distractorRationale.d: Robots are routinely used for heavy loads; the question is about variety, not load capacity.

questions.explanation: A robot's capital cost is shared among all part families, while dedicated loaders multiply with the number of families. Variety is the factor that tips the choice toward the robot.

questions.stem: A dedicated line costs 480 000 currency units (cu) with a 6 year life and no residual value, with variable cost 0.25 cu per part. A programmable cell costs 180 000 cu over the same 6 years with variable cost 0.85 cu per part. Ignoring interest, find the annual quantity in parts per year at which the two options cost the same.
questions.explanation: The annual fixed costs are 80 000 cu and 30 000 cu. Setting $80000+0.25Q=30000+0.85Q$ gives $Q=50000/0.60\approx83300$ parts per year, above which the dedicated line is cheaper.

questions.stem: A robot loader costs 120 000 cu with an 8 year life (no residual value). A dedicated loader for one part family costs 24 000 cu with a 6 year life; each extra family needs its own. Ignoring operating costs and interest, at how many part families (a real number) are the annual costs equal?
questions.explanation: The robot costs $120000/8=15000$ cu per year; each dedicated loader costs $24000/6=4000$ cu per year. Equating $4000n=15000$ gives $n=3.75$ families, so four or more families favour the robot.

questions.stem: A robot loads and unloads a press in 14 s per part cycle. The cell is available 90% of an 8 hour shift (the rest is lost to faults and changeover). Find the number of parts the cell can make in one shift, assuming the robot cycle is the limit.
questions.explanation: Available time is $8\times3600\times0.90=25920$ s. Dividing by 14 s per part gives $25920/14\approx1851$ parts per shift.

questions.stem: A company expects to make 1.5 million identical drink-bottle caps a year for ten years, and another product family of 60 variants, each at 2 000 per year, that changes design every 2 years. Recommend an automation level for each, justifying by volume, variety and changeover cost, and state one risk of your recommendation.
markingGuide: Caps: fixed (dedicated) automation because very high volume and one stable design
Justification: high fixed cost is spread over a huge quantity giving the lowest unit cost
Variants: programmable or flexible automation (CNC or reprogrammable cells) because high variety and low volume per variant
Notes dedicated tooling would be obsolete when the design changes every 2 years
Risk for caps: no ability to change design without retooling; or demand falling leaves investment stranded
Risk for variants: higher unit cost or changeover time losses
questions.explanation: Quantity and variety map directly onto the automation level: very high volume of one design justifies fixed automation, while many variants in modest volumes need reprogrammable machines. The main risk for fixed automation is inflexibility; for the variants it is higher unit cost and changeover losses.

questions.stem: Compare an industrial robot with dedicated tooling for loading parts into a machine, covering speed, cost for one part versus many part families, and response to a design change. State which classification of automation each best illustrates.
markingGuide: Dedicated tooling is faster and cheaper for one product
Robot is slower per move but reprogrammable and can change grippers
Robot's capital cost is shared across families so it wins as the number of families rises
Dedicated tooling must be rebuilt or replaced with a design change; robot is reprogrammed
Dedicated tooling illustrates fixed automation; the robot illustrates programmable (or flexible if changeover is negligible)
questions.explanation: A dedicated loader gives the least cost and highest speed for an unchanging part, but a robot offsets its slower motion by serving many part families through reprogramming. This is why the robot represents programmable automation and the dedicated loader represents fixed automation.
